li.a: The National WWII Museum: The Italian Resistance and the Ardeatine Caves Massacre
Wilson Quarterly: Murder in the Ardeatine Caves

content.p: On 24 March 1944, a day after partisans bombed a column of German police in the middle of Rome, German security forces drove 335 prisoners and men picked up in the city to a set of abandoned quarries on the Via Ardeatina. They were shot in groups of five, each in the back of the head, and the entrance was then blown up to hide the bodies. None of the dead had anything to do with the bombing. The youngest was 15 and the oldest was over 70.

The killings are known in Italy as the Fosse Ardeatine. They became a landmark of the German occupation, and the court cases that followed stretched over more than fifty years, from 1944 to Erich Priebke's final conviction in 1998.

After the armistice of 1943 the Italian king and government left Rome, and German troops took the capital. Several German police forces operated there. One was the Security Police and SD "Außenkommando" under Herbert Kappler, whose offices in the Via Tasso became a symbol of terror; arrested civilians and resisters were tortured there, according to the research project NS-Täter in Italien. On 16 October 1943 a special unit arrested 1,259 Jews in the Rome ghetto area, and 1,007 of them were deported to Auschwitz.

The Allies landed at Anzio, about 50 kilometres south of Rome, on 22 January 1944, but the front stalled. German troops were drawn away from Rome, while the authorities there reacted more harshly to attacks by the partisan Patriotic Action Groups (GAP). After a German soldier was killed near a bridge, ten imprisoned partisans were shot on 31 January.

The GAP chose 23 March for its largest operation, a date marking 25 years since Mussolini launched the first Fascist body in Milan. A young Communist and former medical student, Rosario Bentivegna, dressed as a street sweeper, pushed a cart filled with explosive into Via Rasella. The National WWII Museum puts the charge at 40 pounds of TNT. Bentivegna later told a United Press International reporter that he lit a pipe, touched it to a fuse and walked away.

The target was the 11th Company of the III Battalion of the SS Police Regiment "Bozen", which marched the same route daily from a shooting range to its barracks. NS-Täter in Italien counts 156 men in the column. Most were recruited from South Tyrol, mainly men between 30 and 45, into an SS-led police unit. The bomb and follow-up blasts killed twenty-seven on the spot, according to that source, and seven more died of wounds, the last on the morning of 24 March: 34 in all. The National WWII Museum gives 28 immediate deaths and cites research by the United States Holocaust Memorial Museum putting the final toll at 42. Two Italian civilians were also killed, one of them 13. Other pages quoted here give 33.

Kurt Mälzer, the German military commander of Rome, was reported by Consul General Eitel Friedrich Moellhausen to have been furious at the scene and to have spoken of blowing up nearby buildings and shooting people. Moellhausen said he asked Kappler to talk Mälzer out of it. Kappler instead set about obtaining authority for a reprisal.

Much of what is known about the next hours rests on testimony at Kappler's trial, which NS-Täter in Italien summarises. Kappler said he spoke by telephone to General Eberhard von Mackensen and that the plan was to use people already sentenced to death or life, or liable to execution after police inquiries. He said a staff officer of Mälzer's told him that Field Marshal Albert Kesselring had issued the order to shoot ten Italians for each dead German within 24 hours, and that his inquiry at Kesselring's headquarters brought the answer that the decision came from higher authority. According to the Rome court's findings, Mälzer told him on 24 March that it came from Hitler. NS-Täter in Italien says the order came from Kesselring or possibly Hitler; the National WWII Museum says Kappler acted after permission from Hitler and that Mälzer, Mackensen and Kesselring supported the reprisal.

The arithmetic mattered. According to the trial reconstruction, about 290 men were available on the evening of 23 March, but many were Jews awaiting deportation and did not fit the categories agreed, and most of those arrested in Via Rasella were released the next morning. Kappler obtained permission to add prisoners from Regina Coeli jail: 3 already sentenced to death, 16 with prison sentences and 23 awaiting trial. Rome's police chief, Pietro Caruso, then made 50 more prisoners available. When another German died of wounds, Kappler added ten Jews brought into jail that morning. The Rome military court later found that raising the figure from 320 to 335 was Kappler's own initiative.

Major Johann Dobek, who commanded the Bozen battalion, apparently refused to let his men do the shooting. Under the arrangements with the army, reprisals were the security police's task, so the Außenkommando carried them out.

The prisoners were taken in trucks on the early afternoon of 24 March to the quarries, which lie near the San Callisto catacombs. The Wilson Quarterly dates the march into the caves to about 3:30 p.m. and says the groups of five went in by torchlight. The Rome court found that five SS men forced five shackled prisoners to kneel while each was shot from behind, after which the SS men fetched the next five. Priebke called out the names and crossed them off a list. Carl Schütz gave orders and supervised; the SS leaders, among them Kappler, Priebke and Schütz, shot first. One officer, Reinhold Wetjen, at first refused to shoot and was persuaded by Kappler, according to NS-Täter in Italien. The Wilson Quarterly, citing Der Spiegel, reports that the men drank beforehand and that some victims were left alive among the dead.

The shooting ended around 20:00. The entrance was dynamited. Of the dead, the National WWII Museum says most were already prisoners, many held for resistance activity, while others had been seized in the streets. It counts 75 Jews. NS-Täter in Italien counts 77 in its biography of Priebke. The caves stayed sealed until after Allied troops entered Rome on 4 June 1944.

Forensic physician Attilio Ascarelli led the exhumation, which began on 26 July 1944, and his team identified 326 of the 335. After liberation an Ardeatine Cave Commission chaired by the mayor of Rome handled the inquiry and burials, according to the CIPDH page. Families formed a committee to put names to the dead, and on 26 April 1947 the National Association of Italian Martyr Families for Homeland Freedom (ANFIM) was founded.

The CIPDH page notes that the victims came from every social class and many parts of the country. Among them, the Wilson Quarterly names the Sardinian folk singer Galvino De Lunas. That magazine also says the motive for the killings is unclear and notes that some writers have pointed to an antisemitic element and others to an attempt to frighten the public as the Allies closed in. These readings are the writers' own and are not findings of a court.

The first trial came before the war ended. In September 1944 Caruso was tried with a colleague, Roberto Occhetto. He was accused, among other things, of handing the 50 prisoners to the Germans. Caruso was sentenced to death and executed on 22 September, and Occhetto got 30 years, according to NS-Täter in Italien.

On 20 November 1946 a British military court sentenced Mälzer and Mackensen to death; the sentences were commuted to life imprisonment. Mälzer died in prison on 24 March 1952, and Mackensen was pardoned and freed on 2 October that year. Kesselring was tried at Venice in 1947 by an Allied military court, found guilty on counts that included the Ardeatine killings and sentenced to death. His sentence was commuted, cut to 21 years in 1948 and he was freed four years later.

Kappler's trial opened in Rome in 1948. The court acquitted him on the killing of 320 people, because it was not proven that he knew the shootings were unlawful and because he had acted on orders. It held the shooting of the other 15 was his own initiative and sentenced him to life, with 15 more years for extorting 50 kilograms of gold from Rome's Jewish community. The judges found that Germany as occupier had a right to a reprisal, but called the executions cruel and the number disproportionate. Appeals failed in 1952 and 1953. Kappler escaped from a Rome military hospital on 15 August 1977, returned to Germany and died at Soltau on 9 February 1978.

Priebke, a deputy of Kappler's, was held by American forces in 1945, escaped a British camp near Rimini in 1946, and reached Argentina in 1948 on a Red Cross passport in the name "Otto Pape", according to NS-Täter in Italien. He lived under his own name in Bariloche, working as a waiter and hotel employee before opening a butcher's shop. In spring 1994 an ABC News team found him there. He admitted being present but denied personal involvement. After Argentine courts disagreed, the Supreme Court ruled for extradition to Italy on 2 November 1995.

His defence was that he had only obeyed orders. A recorded 1974 interview in which Kappler said his men had not been forced to take part undermined it, and testimony from the former SS officer Karl Hass incriminated Priebke. On 1 August 1996 the Rome military court found him guilty but held his acts not punishable on grounds of extenuating circumstances and the statute of limitations. Crowds protested outside the courtroom and the mayor switched off the lights of public buildings. NS-Täter in Italien's page on the massacre describes a 15-year sentence at first instance, which differs from its Priebke biography; the discrepancy is not resolved by the pages read. In October 1996 the Court of Cassation annulled the verdict. On 7 March 1998 the military appeals court gave him life imprisonment, and the Court of Cassation confirmed it on 16 November.

Because of his age he served the sentence under house arrest in Rome. In August 2005, NBC News reported, a judge allowed a police-supervised holiday at a villa on Lake Maggiore, and Priebke, then 92, returned to Rome after protests, including from the Simon Wiesenthal Center. He died in Rome on 11 October 2013, and NS-Täter in Italien says authorities and communities refused burial in both Bariloche and his birthplace Hennigsdorf; a funeral by the Society of Saint Pius X was abandoned amid clashes.

The Wilson Quarterly reports that in 1958 the Italian government locked away the case files and that a 1959 exchange between German officials spoke of putting the "affair" to rest. It says Schütz joined the German intelligence service after the war and Kurt Winden became head of the legal department of a Frankfurt bank; both denied the accusations and were never charged. NS-Täter in Italien also notes that a "cabinet of shame" holding more than 2,000 unprocessed cases, among them Priebke's, was found in 1994.

The partisans were criticised for the bomb. NS-Täter in Italien says historical research and legal inquiries have shown a claim that the Germans had ordered the bombers to give themselves up was unfounded, since no such order was given. Bentivegna was taken to court over the civilian deaths and cleared, according to the National WWII Museum. He did not express regret and defended the bombing as legitimate resistance.

The mausoleum was built to designs by teams led by architects Mario Fiorentino and Giuseppe Perugini, with sculptors Mirko Basaldella and Francesco Coccia. Work began in November 1947 and it opened on the fifth anniversary, 24 March 1949. The bronze gate is Basaldella's, and Coccia's six-metre statue is called The three ages of men. A concrete slab lies over the tombs, and a museum behind the mausoleum shows the context. Every year on 24 March a mass and official speeches mark the day, and school groups visit.

The massacre also stands among reprisals that followed. The National WWII Museum says Kesselring issued a decree on 17 June 1944 holding civilians responsible for acts of resistance, and names Civitella and Sant'Anna di Stazzema among later places devastated.
